fatal_errors: The hypothesis invokes precipitation and grain-boundary structure even though the target comparison concerns homogenized, single-phase FCC single crystals, for which grain-boundary mechanisms are absent and secondary phases are not the intended variable.
It does not reconstruct the controlled [1̄23] single-crystal compression comparison or the temperature- and strain-rate-dependent CRSS measurements.
It misses the principal composition-dependent mediator: local lattice distortion quantified by mean-square atomic displacement and its correlation with extrapolated 0 K solid-solution strength.

It omits both key temperature-dependent mechanisms: low-temperature inertial dulling caused by reduced phonon drag and high-temperature Portevin–Le Chatelier strengthening caused predominantly by Cottrell-type Mn/Fe solute pinning.
The predicted outcome is only an unspecified variation in strength, ductility, and toughness, with no directional predictions relative to the quinary baseline.
The proposed falsification test changes alloying, processing, and precipitation simultaneously, so it cannot identify which mediator or mechanism controls the response.

The cited evidence largely concerns compositionally different alloys, polycrystals, nanostructures, dynamic loading, deliberate precipitation, or simulations of nanowires and therefore does not directly support the proposed mechanism for the specified single-phase single-crystal comparison.
explanation: The response offers a generic SFE–twinning–microstructure hypothesis rather than a testable reconstruction of the study. Its nominal quinary baseline and single-phase FCC boundary provide minimal alignment, but it neither controls initial microstructure nor specifies orientation, temperature, strain rate, CRSS, or composition-resolved predictions. More importantly, precipitation and grain-boundary sliding are incompatible with the central single-crystal comparison. It also fails to address the experimentally supported MSAD-controlled glide resistance, cryogenic inertial dulling, and Mn/Fe-dependent high-temperature PL effect. The evidence is broad background literature rather than direct support, and the falsification rule is nondiscriminating because multiple variables are changed together.
